paragraphs.title: The Restoration of Judah and Judgment of the Nations

easy.explanation: The LORD promised to bring again the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem.
easy.q: What did the LORD promise to bring again to Judah and Jerusalem?

easy.explanation: The nations would be brought down into the valley of Jehoshaphat.
easy.q: Where would the LORD gather and bring down the nations?

easy.explanation: The LORD judged them for scattering His people Israel among the nations.
easy.q: Whom had the nations scattered among the nations?

answers: Because they scattered Israel and parted the LORD’s land
Because they did not build Jerusalem
Because they refused to drink wine
medium.explanation: The passage names scattering Israel and dividing the land as reasons for judgment.
medium.q: Why would the LORD plead with the nations?

medium.explanation: The nations cast lots for the people, treating them as captives to be divided.
medium.q: What does “have cast lots for my people” describe?

answers: A boy was given for a harlot and a girl was sold for wine
The children were sent to study in Jerusalem
The children were immediately returned to their families
medium.explanation: The nations traded the captives for sexual service and wine.
medium.q: What happened to the boy and girl in verse 3?

answers: Judah’s restoration is presented alongside repayment for the nations’ crimes
The judgment concerns only the people of Judah
challenge.explanation: The passage joins God’s restoration of Judah with His judgment of those who oppressed His people.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between Judah’s restoration and the nations’ judgment?

answers: The nations took only silver and gold
They scattered Israel and parted the land
challenge.explanation: The nations scattered Israel and divided the LORD’s land.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that both the people and the land were harmed?

answers: The people were treated as merchandise
The nations cared for the children
challenge.explanation: Casting lots and selling the children shows that captives were treated as objects of trade.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the trading of the children?

paragraphs.title: Retribution Against Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia

answers: Tyre, Zidon, and the coasts of Palestine
easy.explanation: The LORD addresses Tyre, Zidon, and all the coasts of Palestine.
easy.q: To whom is the question “what have ye to do with me” addressed?

easy.explanation: The LORD says, “ye have taken my silver and my gold.”
They sold the children to the Grecians.
easy.q: To whom did they sell the children of Judah and Jerusalem?

medium.explanation: The LORD promised, “swiftly and speedily will I return your recompence.”
medium.q: What did the LORD promise Tyre, Zidon, and Philistia?

answers: The repayment or punishment due to them
medium.explanation: The word refers to the repayment they would receive for their deeds.
medium.q: What does “your recompence” mean in this passage?

answers: So they might be removed far from their border
So they could return to Zion
medium.explanation: The children were sold so that they would be removed far from their border.
medium.q: Why had Judah and Jerusalem been sold to a far country?

answers: Those who harm others will receive repayment for their deeds
challenge.explanation: The LORD promises to return the nations’ recompence upon their own head.
challenge.q: What central principle is shown in this description of recompence?

answers: Both are described as offenses for which the LORD will repay them
Only taking the treasures was considered wrong
The sale is presented as an act of kindness
challenge.explanation: Both the theft and the sale of captives are included in the charge against the nations.
challenge.q: What connection is made between taking treasures and selling Judah’s children?

answers: The recompence will return upon the very people who committed the deeds
Only the rulers will receive the recompence
challenge.explanation: The phrase emphasizes that the punishment will come back upon the offenders themselves.
challenge.q: What does “upon your own head” emphasize?

paragraphs.title: The Nations Summoned to War and Judgment

easy.explanation: The nations are told to proclaim and prepare war.
easy.q: For what are the nations told to prepare?

easy.explanation: They were told to beat plowshares into swords and pruninghooks into spears.
easy.q: What were they to do with their agricultural tools?

easy.explanation: The LORD would sit to judge the nations in the valley of Jehoshaphat.
easy.q: Where would the LORD judge the nations?

answers: The nations were being mobilized for war
The land had become especially fruitful
medium.explanation: The changed tools symbolize preparation for battle.
medium.q: What does turning farming tools into weapons show?

answers: Announce and get ready for war
medium.explanation: The command calls the nations to awaken their warriors and prepare for conflict.
medium.q: What does “Prepare war” mean in this context?

answers: They are gathered there to stand before the LORD’s judgment
medium.explanation: The LORD gathers them there because He will sit to judge them.
medium.q: Why are the nations gathered around the valley of Jehoshaphat?

answers: Even the weak are required to claim strength and prepare for battle
The weak are excused from the war
challenge.explanation: The command presents a total mobilization in which even the weak are expected to join the battle.
challenge.q: What is ironic about “let the weak say, I am strong”?

answers: The valley is the meeting place for judgment
The valley is a refuge from judgment
The valley belongs only to Judah
challenge.explanation: The nations are summoned there, and there the LORD will judge them.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the repeated gathering in the valley?

answers: He will strengthen them to win
He will send them to a distant land
challenge.explanation: The passage says, “thither cause thy mighty ones to come down.”
challenge.q: What will the LORD do in relation to the mighty warriors?

paragraphs.title: War Imagined as Harvest and Grape Pressing

answers: A ripe harvest and a full winepress
easy.explanation: The passage uses images of a ripe harvest and an overflowing winepress.
easy.q: To what are the wickedness and judgment of the nations compared?

easy.explanation: The sun and moon will be darkened, and the stars will withdraw their shining.
easy.q: What will be darkened in the day of the LORD?

answers: A reaper and a grape dresser
easy.explanation: The LORD will be the hope of His people and the strength of Israel.
easy.q: What will the LORD be to His people?

medium.explanation: The ripe harvest indicates that the appointed time for reaping has come.
medium.q: Why is the sickle to be put in?

medium.explanation: The harvest is mature and ready to be reaped.
medium.q: What does “ripe” mean in “the harvest is ripe”?

answers: The abundance of wickedness has brought the time of pressing and punishment
The nations will enjoy the wine
The land will stop producing fruit
medium.explanation: A full press and overflowing vats picture the great amount of wickedness awaiting judgment.
medium.q: How does the image of the winepress explain judgment?

answers: The enormous number of people in the valley
challenge.explanation: The repetition emphasizes the great number gathered in the valley of decision.

answers: They emphasize the power of the day of the LORD and His judgment
They explain the sale of captives
challenge.explanation: The cosmic signs portray the overwhelming power of the LORD’s judgment.
challenge.q: How do the darkened lights and shaking heavens relate to the event?

answers: The judgment of the nations versus the LORD’s protection of His people
The wealth of the nations versus Egypt’s poverty
challenge.explanation: The passage describes judgment while also declaring that the LORD is hope and strength for His people.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast in these verses?

paragraphs.title: Jerusalem’s Holiness and the Abundance of the Land

easy.explanation: The LORD is described as dwelling in Zion, His holy mountain.
easy.q: Where does the LORD dwell according to the passage?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “then shall Jerusalem be holy.”
A fountain will come forth from the house of the LORD and water the valley of Shittim.
easy.q: What will come forth from the house of the LORD?

answers: They will no longer pass through her
medium.explanation: The passage says that no strangers shall pass through Jerusalem anymore.
medium.q: What will happen to strangers in Jerusalem?

answers: Fresh wine or sweet grape juice
medium.explanation: The phrase pictures extraordinary abundance flowing from the mountains.
medium.q: What does “new wine” describe in the phrase “the mountains shall drop down new wine”?

medium.explanation: The passage mentions new wine, flowing milk, and waters in the rivers of Judah.
medium.q: Which things describe the abundance of the land?

answers: Knowing the LORD who dwells in Zion is followed by Jerusalem being holy
Knowing the LORD causes Jerusalem to be destroyed
challenge.explanation: The passage connects recognition of the LORD’s presence in Zion with Jerusalem’s holiness.
challenge.q: What connection is made between knowing the LORD and Jerusalem’s holiness?

answers: Blessing and abundance spreading through the land
challenge.explanation: The fountain waters the valley and forms part of the picture of abundant blessing.
challenge.q: What does the fountain from the house of the LORD symbolize in the passage?

answers: Jerusalem is holy and secure, while strangers no longer pass through it
The strangers are holier than Jerusalem
Jerusalem is abandoned and filled with strangers
challenge.explanation: The city’s holiness is linked with the removal of foreign intrusion.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between strangers and Jerusalem?

paragraphs.title: The Desolation of Egypt and Edom, and Lasting Retribution

easy.explanation: Egypt shall be a desolation, and Edom a desolate wilderness.
easy.q: What will happen to Egypt and Edom?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “But Judah shall dwell for ever.”
The final statement says, “the LORD dwelleth in Zion.”
easy.q: Where does the LORD dwell at the close of the passage?

answers: Because of violence against Judah and the shedding of innocent blood
Because they did not build the temple
medium.explanation: Their desolation is connected with violence against Judah and innocent bloodshed.
medium.q: Why will Egypt and Edom become desolate?

answers: Blood shed from people who were not guilty
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to the blood of people who were innocent of the violence against them.

answers: They will endure forever and from generation to generation
They will be sold to a far country
medium.explanation: Judah will dwell forever, and Jerusalem will endure from generation to generation.
medium.q: What does the passage promise about Judah and Jerusalem?

answers: The desolation of Egypt and Edom versus the enduring life of Judah and Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts the desolation of the guilty nations with the lasting future of Judah and Jerusalem.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast in the final verses?

answers: The LORD will not overlook the bloodshed committed against Judah
The blood will be erased without judgment
Judah will give up any claim for justice
challenge.explanation: The LORD declares that He will address and avenge the bloodshed that has not yet been cleansed.
challenge.q: What does “I will cleanse their blood that I have not cleansed” mean in context?

answers: It connects Judah and Jerusalem’s lasting security with the LORD’s presence
It announces that the LORD is leaving Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The LORD’s dwelling in Zion confirms His continuing presence with and protection of His people.
challenge.q: How does “the LORD dwelleth in Zion” strengthen the passage’s message?
